title: Cranly’s
html_source:
A friend of Stephen’s in A portrait of the artist as a young man, based on Joyce’s friend J. F Byrne.

Stephen and Cranly have a falling out towards the end of the book as Cranly was singing a petition per pax universalis. Stephen is sarcy and cocky and Cranly let’s loose in tone :

‘a flaming bloody sugar is what he is’,

sugar meaning a dead loss (Seamus Deane,Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, Penguin).

Stephen wonders if Cranly will use that phrase about him and then: the heavy lumpish phrase sank slowly out of hearing like a stone through a quagmire. In Giacomo Joyce, it becomes My words in her mind, cold polished stones sinking through a quagmire.

A similar situation occurred between Joyce and J.F. Byrne at UCD when Joyce’s acquaintances signed a petition protesting against the Yeats' play The Countess Cathleen (Ellmann).
